items.title: The world doesn’t need solar or wind — it needs solar and wind
items.summary:
Humans are still hunter gatherers — not for food, but for energy: Much like we once roamed the landscape digging up edible roots, today we gouge the planet for coal, oil, and gas. But just as we eventually adopted agriculture, we’re starting to farm the wind and sun. Because we can’t stop our star from setting, though, we must combine solar panels with large batteries, which load up on energy during the day and distribute it at night. 

According to a new report from the energy think tank Ember, diversifying the electrical grid by adding wind power is a massive opportunity to reduce costs. “If you rely on one crop and that crop is having a bad year, you’re going to be struggling,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember and author of the new report. “The same is true for wind and solar, and it’s the reason why diversification is so important. We’re now building batteries, and those are effectively the silos where we store the sunshine for later in the day.”

The report found that in the United States and Europe, you’d need 20 hours of battery storage to achieve 90 percent uptime for solar. Add wind power to the system and that drops to just 12 hours, meaning you don’t have to install as many costly lithium -ion batteries . Accordingly, worldwide this technique could drop the median cost of meeting that 90 percent demand from $105 per megawatt-hour with solar to $86 with additional wind power. (You can see the potential of that wind power in the map below — it alone can more than meet electricity demand.)

items.t: The world doesn’t need solar or wind — it needs solar and wind

items.title: El Niño is already scrambling your ski season
items.summary:
Being open for Thanksgiving has long been a goal for major ski resorts, including Sugarbush in Vermont. It had planned to have its lifts running and its slopes swarming by now. But with highs approaching 60 degrees Fahrenheit for much of the past week, that hasn’t happened.

”It’s been a really warm November,” said John Bleh, director of communications at Sugarbush. “New snow-making technology has helped a ton, but it’s not the ultimate cure-all.”

The popular destination is one of a slew throughout the East, from Sugarloaf in Maine to Snowshoe Mountain in West Virginia, that have had to delay opening due to unseasonably balmy conditions.

On the other side of the country, skiers in California are gloating. Resorts in the Lake Tahoe area received more than 4 feet of snow after a recent series of storms. The bounty was so generous that the Sierra Avalanche Center was warning of a “considerable” risk of slides and Kirkwood Mountain Resort opened nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. “It’s always exciting to get the season underway, but being able to open this early is a huge win,” Ricky Newberry, the resort’s general manager, said in a statement .

It’s a bit more complicated in the Rockies. Some resorts in Utah and Colorado got off to a slow start before recent storms brought snow, but Wolf Creek in the southern end of the state has opened all of its terrain . 

These wildly different starts to the ski season are a clear sign that the “super” or “Godzilla” El Niño, the strongest on record, is already shaping what could be a weird winter on the slopes.

El Niño occurs every…
items.t: El Niño is already scrambling your ski season

items.title: How wildfire litigation became big business in America
items.summary:
On a November morning in 2018, the foothills of the Sierra Nevada were primed to burn. Northern California had received little rainfall, and the grasses and shrubs above the town of Paradise were bone dry. Humidity levels were dangerously low as winds up to 40 miles per hour gusted downslope toward the 26,000-person community.

When a live wire broke free from a 99-year-old transmission tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Paradise stood little chance. 

The arcing wire ignited the brush below to start the Camp Fire, which claimed the lives of 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures in a matter of hours, charring whole neighborhoods to displace tens of thousands of people. It was the deadliest wildfire in California’s history.

But another metric would later come to define the fire that destroyed Paradise.

Thousands of victims sued PG&E. The utility eventually agreed to settle their claims for $13.5 billion in compensation for the Camp Fire, as well as other blazes ignited by its equipment in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. It was one of the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history, driving the company to bankruptcy and demonstrating that utilities could be held liable for huge sums when faulty equipment ignites conflagrations. 

The settlement sparked a wave of lawsuits against utilities implicated in wildfire ignitions across the country. Today, wildfire litigation is a multibillion-dollar business in the U.S., with more than $18 billion awarded or agreed to in civil settlements for victims in California, Hawaiʻi,…
items.t: How wildfire litigation became big business in America

items.title: ‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat
items.summary:
Temperatures in a concrete facility contributed to one man’s death after he struggled to breathe, prisoners allege

On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”

Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,”…
items.t: ‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat

items.title: New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant
items.summary:
Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm , a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings.

Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid.

In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant ; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most. 

“This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers.

The initiative ​“should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​“DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity prices are likely to be highest, ​“a neat part about the virtual power plant is you don’t have to…
items.t: New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant

items.title: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states
items.summary:
It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose.

A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. In Virginia and Iowa, data centers consumed 15.5 and 13.1 percent, respectively.

Hyperscale data centers used nearly one-fifth of Oregon’s…
items.t: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states

items.title: Is it OK to want a ‘normal life’ during the climate crisis?
items.summary:
“I would love to be a parent, but I worry it is unethical to bring children into a world that is wrecked by climate change.” 

“It feels kind of silly to be bothering with working a normal job and planning for retirement in some distant future, given the overall circumstances.” 

“Sometimes I feel hypocritical, working toward a better, more sustainable future while not fully reflecting those values in my own daily choices.” 

“My partner and I are thinking about buying our first home together and becoming parents. How can I make plans for the future in a world that is unravelling?” 

In the many questions we’ve received through the Ask a Climate Therapist form , I’ve noticed a theme running through several of them. People longing to have children, but grappling with the ethics of that decision. People wanting to enjoy occasional travel or an omnivorous diet, but feeling the sting of guilt. People hoping to plan for retirement or home ownership, but unsure how to reconcile those long-term visions with their fears and doubts about our climate future.

I’d sum it up like this: Knowing what we know about the climate crisis, and knowing that we each must do our part to contribute to a liveable future, is it OK to want to enjoy life, too?

Ask a Climate Therapist tackles your questions about how to navigate the emotional side of climate change, with leading climate-aware therapist Leslie Davenport. Have a question? Ask it here ! 

Climate change is a systemic problem, but the choices we make in our own lives still matter as we push for large-scale change. Some choices are more…
items.t: Is it OK to want a ‘normal life’ during the climate crisis?

“That surge shot directly at us,” said Goodman, 67, describing how the river takes a sharp 90-degree turn near his and his sister’s house in one of the Navajo housing authority’s residential neighborhoods. It just missed the house by about 50ft, he said.

The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

items.title: Even the ‘good guys’ of AI are locking in fossil fuels
items.summary:
Anthropic became one of the most valuable companies on the planet on Wednesday, valued at $1.5 trillion after its IPO. Known as one of the “good guys” of AI , Anthropic was founded by employees who left OpenAI over disagreements about ethics and safety. But despite the company’s emphasis on responsibility and preventing AI from killing everybody, one thing you don’t hear Anthropic talking about much is its contribution to climate change. 

Ahead of the initial public offering this week, Greenpeace accused the company of “asking average investors to join them in throwing the planet into the climate furnace.” AI data centers are causing electricity demand to soar and fueling a surge in natural gas plants . A recent report found that the biggest data centers in the United States emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark. Anthropic is contributing to that: It reportedly signed a $3.4 billion deal with the Texas-based company OnePWR Solutions in September to power data centers with gas-fired engines — the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab.

“It signals what direction they’re taking very clearly,” said Charlie Cray, a senior strategist at Greenpeace USA. The company is locking in fossil fuels at a time when scientists say the world is certain to overshoot the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees C . Anthropic’s reputation for being the most responsible of the AI giants means it should be minimizing its climate impact, Cray argued: “Show the world that you can do it better.”

The company has been lauded for…
items.t: Even the ‘good guys’ of AI are locking in fossil fuels

items.title: As black lung disease surges, the Trump administration proposes ‘deregulatory’ protections for miners
items.summary:
Coal mining is dangerous and takes a toll on the body, but a miner working underground can earn enough to buy a house, drive a nice car, and send the kids to college. There was a time when John Robinson thought the trade-off was worth it. No longer. He was diagnosed with black lung disease at age 47, a consequence of inhaling toxic silica dust in the mines of Virginia.

“These companies will bait you in with this big money,” said Robinson, who is now 60 and vice president of the National Black Lung Association. “When you get down and out, well, guess what? You’re like an old wore-out tire on the car or something. They’ll throw you to the side ’cause you ain’t worth nothing.”

For more than 50 years, coal miners, their families, and advocates have pressed the federal government for stricter limits on silica exposure, stronger enforcement of rules meant to protect miners, and improved health benefits for those disabled by the disease. In 2024, the Biden administration set the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica at 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, matching the Occupational Safety and Health Administration threshold for workers in other industries. The rule was finalized in 2024, with coal companies required to comply beginning in April 2025.

That regulation was meant to update protections in coal mines and in what regulators call metal and nonmetal mines, which extract everything from copper and critical minerals to stone, sand, and gravel. All of them carry a risk of inhaling silica dust, whose fine particles can lodge deep in the lungs. But…
items.t: As black lung disease surges, the Trump administration proposes ‘deregulatory’ protections for miners
